title: UnF*ck Your Cold Email: Beating AI Spam Filters with Taylor Haren
speakers_and_attribution: Adam Robinson hosts with Pete, who describes his RB2B production role and new fractional marketing business, Market Work. Taylor Haren is the principal cold-email guest; captions also render his surname as Harren and his business as salesmation.systems. Eric Tabone, introduced as representing Nearshore Businesses, gives the opening hiring-services pitch. Most infrastructure, campaign-performance, personalization and sequencing claims belong to Taylor, including results he reports for RB2B. Pete supplies much of the marketing commentary and questioning. Speaker identification is inferred from conversational context because the captions are not diarized. Uncertain host turns are explicitly qualified.
summary: Taylor describes RB2B's restarted outbound campaigns, high-volume sending infrastructure, data enrichment, deliverability diagnostics, copy testing, personalization and sequencing. His central recommendation is to improve the offer and test a strong first email, while retaining follow-ups when evidence supports them. Claims about AI spam filtering and warm-up mechanisms are explicitly speculative or anecdotal. Adam contributes questions, a historical RB2B conversion recollection, a hands-on infrastructure anecdote and visible support for Pete's move into fractional work. The opening covers Latin American hiring and Pete's business; the closing covers employee entrepreneurship, LinkedIn visibility and ongoing public reporting about RB2B's email performance.

key_learnings.claim: Eric positions nearshore hiring as a way to access senior engineering, sales and professional-services talent as well as administrative support.
key_learnings.speaker: Eric Tabone
key_learnings.caveat: Sales-pitch claims about Eric's service; these are not Adam's hiring outcomes or independently assessed talent comparisons.

key_learnings.claim: Pete's fractional marketing offer addresses companies that need experiment design, messaging and guidance for junior staff but lack capacity for a full-time senior marketer.
key_learnings.speaker: Pete
key_learnings.caveat: Pete describes a soft-launch offer, with more structured deliverables still under consideration.

key_learnings.claim: Taylor restarted RB2B with essentially the same list and copy to establish a control before optimizing, and says the old approach still performed surprisingly well.
key_learnings.speaker: Taylor Haren
key_learnings.caveat: An operational comparison, not a randomized experiment. The list was reverified, and elapsed time and market conditions could affect results.

key_learnings.claim: Taylor delays increasing send volume while testing copy so he can avoid changing two major variables simultaneously.
key_learnings.speaker: Taylor Haren
key_learnings.caveat: Describes his RB2B testing decision at the time; later volume targets are plans, not completed results.

key_learnings.claim: Taylor observes what he calls copy fatigue at higher sending volumes and hypothesizes that providers detect the overall sales character of messages, beyond individual keywords.
key_learnings.speaker: Taylor Haren
key_learnings.caveat: He explicitly says he lacks proof of the AI-filter explanation. The video title is stronger than the demonstrated evidence.

key_learnings.claim: Taylor's RB2B infrastructure spreads outbound traffic across many Gmail accounts and domains, using Instantly for sending.
key_learnings.speaker: Taylor Haren
key_learnings.caveat: A July 2025 operating configuration, not a universal or durable provider limit.

key_learnings.claim: Taylor distinguishes ordinary domain administration from very large-scale operations: he considers registrar-plus-Cloudflare management workable below his extreme scale, but recounts losing account-management access with 15,000 domains.
key_learnings.speaker: Taylor Haren
key_learnings.caveat: His account incident is anecdotal. Existing DNS records and email accounts continued functioning, so this was not the immediate disappearance of every sending domain.

key_learnings.claim: Domain infrastructure has recurring costs and administrative work beyond introductory registration prices; Taylor links this burden to demand for his managed infrastructure service.
key_learnings.speaker: Taylor Haren
key_learnings.caveat: Prices are illustrative. His claim that domains older than a year deliver best is an unverified practitioner observation.

key_learnings.claim: Taylor generates sending-domain names from a client root plus prefixes and suffixes, and added checks after a combination accidentally produced an inappropriate phrase.
key_learnings.speaker: Taylor Haren
key_learnings.caveat: His broad assertion that nobody examines domain names is opinion; he supplies his own exception.

key_learnings.claim: Taylor rotates infrastructure sets during the month and cools inactive sets, but cannot substantiate whether using Adam's name improves performance over other sender names.
key_learnings.speaker: Taylor Haren
key_learnings.caveat: He initially believes the name helps, then acknowledges lacking a direct comparison. Captions say Alex at one point despite the question referring to Adam.

key_learnings.claim: Pete cautions that most attendees do not need Taylor's sending scale; Taylor gives a qualified endorsement of purchasing infrastructure through sending platforms for ordinary users.
key_learnings.speaker: Pete and Taylor Haren
key_learnings.caveat: Pete supplies the scale boundary. Taylor says he has not directly tested the platform-provided infrastructure and relies partly on friends' experiences.

key_learnings.claim: Taylor uses two weeks of warm-up as a precaution but thinks its main value is ongoing maintenance of complaint ratios rather than a necessary initial preparation period.
key_learnings.speaker: Taylor Haren
key_learnings.caveat: The mechanism is his theory, supported by a friend's reported experiment. He explicitly distinguishes Gmail from Outlook and says Outlook does require warm-up.

key_learnings.claim: Taylor keeps warm-up active during outbound campaigns, while disagreeing with Pete's emphasis on mimicking ordinary human email engagement.
key_learnings.speaker: Taylor Haren, responding to Pete
key_learnings.caveat: The practice is self-reported; the proposed explanation of its effectiveness is not established.

key_learnings.claim: Taylor treats reply-rate declines as a warning signal, not a diagnosis: copy and other factors can also explain them. He combines this with blacklist checks and inconclusive warm-up health scores.
key_learnings.speaker: Taylor Haren
key_learnings.caveat: The specific blacklist-checking site is not named in the spoken transcript. He says inbox-placement tests have not matched his observed results.

key_learnings.claim: Taylor plans to classify bounce logs into server errors, invalid addresses and suspected-spam blocks so deterioration can be diagnosed more precisely.
key_learnings.speaker: Taylor Haren
key_learnings.caveat: The analytics feature is planned or being built, not shown as operational. The percentage example is hypothetical.

key_learnings.claim: Adam asks how outbound volume relates to the actual addressable market, prompting Taylor to explain that Fixer's broad Gmail-and-Outlook audience is an exceptional case.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson and Taylor Haren
key_learnings.caveat: Adam poses the question; Taylor supplies the strategy and numbers. The stated TAM and contact-cycle arithmetic are unresolved.

key_learnings.claim: Taylor uses a data waterfall starting with Apollo, followed by validation, Lead Magic and a final provider captioned as Wiza/WISA/Wizo; previously excluded records reportedly added valuable responses.
key_learnings.speaker: Taylor Haren
key_learnings.caveat: Provider spellings and validator names vary in the captions. The final data provider is also Taylor's client, and the experiment's denominator is unclear.

key_learnings.claim: Pete frames marketing effectiveness as matching the message, recipient and medium: infrastructure enables delivery, while a defined ICP and relevant message determine the remaining opportunity.
key_learnings.speaker: Pete
key_learnings.caveat: This is Pete's stated philosophy, not Adam's. His analogy between personal inbox triage and AI filters is speculative.

key_learnings.claim: Taylor reports that changing the capitalization of AI in a client's copy coincided with reply performance collapsing and reversing the change coincided with recovery.
key_learnings.speaker: Taylor Haren
key_learnings.caveat: An anecdotal before-and-after observation, not proof of causality. The visual typography demonstration cannot be fully recovered from captions.

key_learnings.claim: Taylor resumed using Mail Meteor alongside Email Guard after an employee's small copy experiment improved replies; he now checks both flagged words and a broader spam score.
key_learnings.speaker: Taylor Haren
key_learnings.caveat: The workflow changed shortly before recording. Third-party scores are not direct evidence of Google or Microsoft's filter logic.

key_learnings.claim: A drop in recorded replies can reflect disconnected inboxes and missing response capture, rather than poorer copy or delivery.
key_learnings.speaker: Taylor Haren
key_learnings.caveat: Taylor gives this explanation for that day's lower displayed campaign result; no completed repair or reconciled result is provided.

key_learnings.claim: Taylor favors AI personalization that identifies whom the prospect sells to or describes relevant uses of saved time, rather than conspicuous company-name insertion or unrelated personal trivia.
key_learnings.speaker: Taylor Haren
key_learnings.caveat: He had retained a company-name variable to preserve a historical control despite disliking it; removal was planned.

key_learnings.claim: Taylor thinks RB2B's genuinely ongoing free tier helps its outbound offer remain attractive despite competing products.
key_learnings.speaker: Taylor Haren
key_learnings.caveat: An explanation proposed by the service provider, not an isolated test of free-tier effects or a statement establishing competitors' actual terms.

key_learnings.claim: RB2B's campaign asks recipients to reply for a signup link, but Taylor says many instead navigate directly to the website; reply metrics therefore undercount associated signups.
key_learnings.speaker: Taylor Haren
key_learnings.caveat: The signup attribution method and measurement window are not supplied.

key_learnings.claim: Adam says using RB2B to reach people already interested in RB2B has an inherent relevance advantage, qualifying the unusually strong historical conversion result.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: This concerns an RB2B-triggered audience and should not be generalized to ordinary cold prospecting.

key_learnings.claim: Pete favors personalization that articulates the recipient's pain precisely. Taylor agrees for targeted outreach but prefers broad product relevance at very high volume, where individual pain diagnosis is harder.
key_learnings.speaker: Pete and Taylor Haren
key_learnings.caveat: A scale-dependent disagreement, not a shared universal rule. Taylor's prediction that AI will eventually do both is prospective.

key_learnings.claim: Taylor argues that headline reply rates can be misleading without sequence length and response sentiment, since repeated follow-ups can increase requests to stop.
key_learnings.speaker: Taylor Haren
key_learnings.caveat: His illustrative percentages are not results from a specified client campaign.

key_learnings.claim: Taylor generally prefers one strong email to the TAM every one or two months, but tests a second step for every new client and retains exceptions for analytical buyers or useful storytelling.
key_learnings.speaker: Taylor Haren
key_learnings.caveat: His cybersecurity client performs better on the second email. His recommendation is shaped by his agency's high-volume model.

key_learnings.claim: Taylor is building a performance database intended to help future models generate individual emails from prior results, potentially reducing reliance on manually written campaigns.
key_learnings.speaker: Taylor Haren
key_learnings.caveat: A development direction and forecast. He explicitly says the models are not yet ready and gives no demonstrated end-to-end implementation.

key_learnings.claim: Taylor concludes that the offer is the largest driver of campaign performance and that small copy changes cannot compensate for a weak underlying proposition.
key_learnings.speaker: Taylor Haren
key_learnings.caveat: This does not erase his earlier emphasis on functioning delivery infrastructure. The opening teaser repeats this same passage.

key_learnings.claim: Taylor says Adam has asked him to post monthly about cold-email results and problems, including a pending explanation of the recent infrastructure failure.
key_learnings.speaker: Taylor Haren
key_learnings.caveat: Guest-reported reporting arrangement. Taylor says the cause was found but does not disclose it in this transcript.

backstory_and_values.claim: Adam says Taylor handles their email and that they have done well from it.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Adam Robinson
backstory_and_values.caveat: A qualitative endorsement without a defined financial return or measurement period.

backstory_and_values.claim: Adam invites Pete to explain his new fractional work, offer and reception because members of the audience aspire to similar work.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Adam Robinson
backstory_and_values.caveat: A concrete on-show action supporting Pete's visibility; it does not establish a general employment policy.

backstory_and_values.speaker: Pete
backstory_and_values.caveat: Pete's career history, not Adam's. Market Work was in soft launch.

backstory_and_values.speaker: Likely Adam Robinson
backstory_and_values.caveat: The captions do not firmly distinguish Adam from Pete in this exchange; retain provisional attribution.

backstory_and_values.claim: Taylor praises an employee for running a limited independent experiment and bringing data after Taylor initially deferred reviewing the idea.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Taylor Haren
backstory_and_values.caveat: Taylor's management preference, not Adam's. He frames approval around a small experiment he believed would cause no harm.

backstory_and_values.speaker: Taylor Haren
backstory_and_values.caveat: Relative timing is tied to recording, whose exact date is not supplied; this is Taylor's backstory.

backstory_and_values.claim: Taylor says he values employees starting businesses and interprets Adam's enthusiasm for Pete's move as a similar attitude.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Taylor Haren
backstory_and_values.caveat: The explicit general value statement is Taylor's. Adam's support is Taylor's interpretation plus observable on-show encouragement.

backstory_and_values.speaker: Adam Robinson
backstory_and_values.caveat: Adam wonders whether the dinner preceded or influenced her posting; he does not establish causality. The guest's name is garbled in captions.

tensions_and_corrections: Taylor, not Adam, supplies most of the episode's technical strategies and business metrics. His agency revenue, staffing, infrastructure and career history must remain separate from Adam's wiki proof.
The title presents AI spam filters as established; Taylor initially labels his explanation a theory without proof. Later confident language does not supply the missing verification.
The early 20% reply and 21.5% positive figures lack consistent denominators. Later references to 1.3% replies and 250 sends per positive cannot be silently harmonized with them.

Taylor first describes roughly a year since contacting the list, then specifies a late-November-to-May pause of about six months. The original copy may be a year old even though the pause was shorter.

The May restart, two-week infrastructure failure, two-week rebuild, two weeks of resumed volume and closing reference to last month's failure lack an exact shared chronology. Publication date is not a verified recording date.
Taylor explicitly corrects the 8.5-million-email client from RB2B to Fixer. Elsewhere the discussion uses 8.2 million and a host rounds to eight million; preserve those variants.
Fixer's stated 1.37-million-person TAM, monthly sending in excess of eight million and two-year full-market contact cycle do not reconcile as spoken.

Historical one-per-nine performance is clarified as signups per sent email, although Adam introduces the question using positive-reply language. The current 38-to-1 ratio is not defined equally clearly.

Taylor says the same copy still works, but later reports recent spam-word changes and an impending set of new variants. The unchanged-copy claim describes the restart control, not every subsequent campaign.
Taylor doubts the conventional rationale for warm-up but still uses an initial precautionary period and continuous warm-up. He also supplies an Outlook-specific exception.
The warm-up complaint example mixes total-message and outbound-message denominators. It should remain an unverified explanation rather than a corrected formula.
Pete explains warm-up through simulated engagement; Taylor emphasizes complaint dilution. These are distinct proposed mechanisms.
Taylor's lower displayed reply rate on the recording day is attributed to disconnected inboxes, demonstrating that observed metrics can reflect collection failures.
Taylor generally rejects extensive follow-up sequences but tests a second step for each new client and retains a cybersecurity example where it performs better.
Pete emphasizes precise pain-point personalization; Taylor limits his alternative approach to high-volume campaigns with broadly applicable products.
Taylor's offer-first conclusion coexists with his requirement for working deliverability. The episode does not support ignoring infrastructure.
Taylor's Cloudflare account-management failure involving 15,000 domains is distinct from the later RB2B sending-infrastructure burn. The transcript does not establish a common cause.
The closing claim that the infrastructure failure was understood does not explain its cause; it remains an open item for future reporting.

Captions contain inconsistent company, provider and personal names, including Fixer, Wiza/WISA/Wizo, Bounceban/debounce, Taylor's company and the Hootsuite guest. These have not been silently repaired.
No substantive financing history, VC comparison, approved mission or calibrated writing-voice evidence is established in this episode.
